units.translation: (Bothius rightly deleted γ', perhaps not read in M, but added only in the copies, not suitable to this passage)
[ἄγαν [too much] introduced by a copyist's error Eum. 944 εὐθενοῦντ᾽ ἄγαν [flourishing too much] for εὐθενοῦντα γα [flourishing, earth], which Dobraeus restored.]
Do not fear the crowd of newcomers too much.
Thus they were killing with sisterly hands too much.
With self-willed judgment he reveres mortals too much.
to frighten too much with words.
I know the Greek tongue too well.
an eye that sees and is not too much closed.
You are too soft toward the Greeks.
Know not to revere human things too much.
Do not hear openly, hear too much.
even if he is too talkative.
A raw-biting desire urges you too much.
Too true are the visions of dream phantoms.
The heart, too evil-prophesying, is troubled.
But you judged these things too lightly.
How too heavy on your feet you came.
The female boundary is too persuasive.
Why did you utter this too piercing word?
And dead, he is not too free.
And they are too maddened with unholy rage, natural-minded.
(Doric for ἀγηνόρειος) same as ἀγήνωρ, brave
A word not read elsewhere, which Meineke in vain changed to ἄγαν ἄρειος [too warlike] in his note on Theocritus p. 396.
The same adjective seems to lie hidden in the corrupt reading
where Hermann corrected to δίδυμα ἀγανόρεα κακὰ | αὐτοφόνα [twin manly evils, self-slain], to which perhaps should be preferred what Weil conjectured: δίδυμ᾽ ἀγανόρει᾽ ἄχη [twin manly griefs].
CHORUS: The Ionian people is not one that flees from battle. XERXES: Manly.
double cares, twin (M has διδύμ' from the first hand) ανορέα (thus M, not ἀγανορέα as printed in Poet. scen. p. 22) self-slain evils,
gentle, mild. Of sacrifices portending favorable things
Thus Weil corrected what is in M: ἀγανὰ φαίνεις [you show gentle things].
From sacrifices a gentle hope appearing wards off insatiable care.
Why do we delay, loudly groaning?
Hesychius: ἀγαστά [admirable things]: things one would admire, such as pleasing things.
admirable things: things one would admire, such as pleasing things
Frequent in Homer as an epithet of heroes: see Thes. vol. 1 p. 224.
(thus from one copy for λιπών [having left]).
whence in line 16 Brunck rightly restored Αγβατάνων [of Ecbatana] for Εκβατάνων [of Ecbatana]. For Αγβάτανα [Ecbatana] is the older form of the name, on which see L. Dindorf in Thes. vol. 3 p. 375.
the city of Susa and Ecbatana
